passage:
'You didn't come to the aarti tonight,' Binita said, sitting on the edge of Tanuja's hostel bed.
'I couldn't. I stood outside and the bells sounded like noise.'
'Because of Aji?'
'I prayed every day she was in hospital, Binita. Every single day. And she still died. So either nobody's listening, or...' Tanuja stopped.
'Or what?'
'I don't know. That's the problem. I don't know anything anymore.'
Binita was quiet for a bit. 'My mother went through something like this when my uncle died. She didn't go to the temple for a year.'
'And then?'
'Then she started reading, and talking to the old priest at our temple, who told her even saints argued with God. She goes again now, but differently.'
'I don't want to pretend I'm fine with it.'
'Then don't. Just don't decide everything this week.'
Tanuja pulled the blanket around her shoulders. 'Maybe I'll talk to our family pandit-ji when I go home. Just talk.'

qa.q: Who died while Tanuja was praying every day?
qa.a: Aji died while Tanuja was praying every day.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she stood outside the aarti?
qa.a: Tanuja felt empty and lost, the bells sounding like noise after Aji's death despite her prayers.

qa.q: What small step does Tanuja decide on, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To talk to the family pandit-ji at home, which keeps her honest about the doubt while seeking an elder's help.

qa.q: Why might Binita share her mother's story?
qa.a: Binita wants Tanuja to know that doubt after a loss is common and can change shape over time.

grounding: Shows prayer feeling empty after a grandmother's death, and the wise path of staying honest about doubt, not forcing certainty, and talking to an elder.

passage: I'm Sarika, and the winter my brother died in a bike accident, I stopped being able to pray. I'd sit before the little shrine in our Pune flat, fold my hands, and feel nothing, like shouting into an empty well. Amma kept saying, 'Have faith, it was his time,' and I wanted to scream. My college is a Christian college with a chapel I had walked past for two years, and one evening I finally went in, just because it was quiet. The chaplain, Father Francis, found me there. I told him I wasn't even Christian. He smiled and said that didn't matter, and that some of the psalms are just people shouting at God. He showed me one. It was angrier than anything I'd dared to say. I read the Gita that month too, and some of it made me cry. I still don't know what I believe. But I've stopped pretending I'm certain, and prayer feels less like a lie.

qa.q: Where did Sarika go one evening because it was quiet?
qa.a: Sarika went into the college chapel.

qa.q: What did prayer feel like to Sarika after the death?
qa.a: Prayer felt empty, like shouting into an empty well, leaving Sarika numb and angry.

qa.q: What helped Sarika stay honest rather than force certainty?
qa.a: Talking to Father Francis, reading angry psalms and the Gita, and letting the questions stay open.

qa.q: What might Amma have meant by 'it was his time'?
qa.a: Amma was likely trying to comfort herself and Sarika through her own faith, though it hurt Sarika to hear.

grounding: A first-person account of prayer feeling empty after a brother's death, and doubt deepening through honest reading and talking to an elder rather than forced certainty.

passage:

Manjula: you ok?
Jagdish: honestly no. I'm angry. at God. is that allowed
Jagdish: we did everything right. Papa did seva every Sunday for 20 yrs. and the fire took the whole shop anyway
Manjula: I think you're allowed to be angry
Jagdish: everyone at home keeps saying 'it's His will' and I just nod
Jagdish: inside I'm screaming
Manjula: my nani used to say even the prayers she learnt as a kid have lines that argue with God
Manjula: maybe you don't have to swallow it

Manjula: that's what scares me a bit. can you say it out loud to someone there? the granthi-ji you like?
Jagdish: maybe. he always has time after the evening prayer
Manjula: go tomorrow. and call me after

passage: After the flood took the family's cotton field and their only cow, Sonali stopped going to the Hanuman temple at the edge of her village in Vidarbha. Every evening her mother lit the lamp at home and folded her hands, and every evening Sonali left the room. Sonali had done nothing wrong, and neither had her parents. At the canal one evening, the priest's son Vijay, who had been at school with her, sat down nearby. 'You look like you want to throw stones at the temple bell.' 'I do,' Sonali said. 'We prayed. We fasted. And the river came anyway.' Vijay didn't argue. 'My father says the old women's songs at the temple are half complaints to God. Come on Tuesday when they sing. You don't have to pray. Just shout with them.' On Tuesday Sonali sat at the back of the temple courtyard. The songs were full of 'why'. She cried, for the first time since the flood.

qa.q: What did the flood take?
qa.a: The flood took the family's cotton field and their only cow.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling toward the temple?
qa.a: Sonali felt angry at God, wanting to throw stones at the temple bell because the prayers had not helped.

qa.q: What did Vijay suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Joining the women's songs full of complaint on Tuesday, which let her anger speak inside the community instead of being bottled up.

qa.q: How does Sonali's mother seem to cope after the flood?
qa.a: Her mother keeps lighting the lamp and praying each evening, finding steadiness in her faith.

grounding: Shows anger at God after a flood the family did not deserve, and a friend guiding Sonali to let the protest speak within the community's songs.

passage: In their small town near Bankura, Bidisha's father, Shankar, heard from a neighbour that she hadn't kept the Shivratri fast at her college hostel. That evening he sat on the verandah without eating. 'Is this what the city teaches? Next you'll stop touching your grandmother's feet.' Bidisha felt her face burn. A sharp answer was ready: that fasting was just habit. She had said something like it to a friend once and hated how it sounded. Instead she sat on the step below him. 'Baba, I have questions. I'm reading, I'm thinking. But I haven't stopped loving you or Thakuma, and I haven't stopped being honest or kind. Those came from you.' He looked at the tulsi plant, not at her. 'And the puja?' 'I'll help Ma prepare it on Sunday, like always. I may not believe everything the way you do. I'll still be there.' After a long while, he picked up his plate.

qa.q: How did Shankar find out about the fast?
qa.a: Shankar heard from a neighbour.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when her father spoke?
qa.a: Bidisha felt her face burn with hurt and embarrassment, and was tempted to answer sharply.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say that eased her father's fear?
qa.a: That she still loved him and Thakuma, still held the values they taught, and would help with Sunday's puja, sharing her questions gently.

qa.q: What is Shankar afraid of?
qa.a: Shankar fears the city is pulling Bidisha away from the family's ways and values.

grounding: Shows a father afraid that his daughter's questions mean losing her values, and her reassuring him of her love while sharing doubts without contempt for the rituals.

passage: When I started asking questions at our temple study circle, it went quiet fast. I'm Ojas, and I was nineteen. I asked, politely I thought, why women in our circle weren't allowed to read certain texts aloud. The uncle who led the circle said, 'This is not the place for arguments.' The next week, two boys I'd grown up with stopped saving me a seat. At the festival, people nodded at my parents and not at me. I felt so lonely I almost walked out for good, and I wrote a long angry post that I thankfully never sent. What saved it was Nandini-aunty, who ran the temple library. She found me sulking by the shoe stand and said, 'Your question is an old one. Come on Thursday; I'll show you three saints who asked it.' I did. I still go on Thursdays. I don't win every argument. I just have one person there I can ask anything.

qa.q: Who ran the temple library?
qa.a: Nandini-aunty ran the temple library.

qa.q: What did Ojas feel when the boys stopped saving a seat?
qa.a: Ojas felt lonely and rejected, close to walking out for good.

qa.q: What turned things around for Ojas?
qa.a: Finding one open-minded elder, Nandini-aunty, and going to her Thursday sessions instead of cutting all ties.

qa.q: How might the uncle who led the circle have seen Ojas's question?
qa.a: The uncle seems to have seen it as an argument that threatened the circle, not as an honest question.

grounding: A spoken account of a temple circle going cold after honest questions, and finding one open-minded elder instead of cutting all ties in anger.

passage:
Sunday: At the youth group after mass in Mangaluru, Vikas asked why a loving God would shut out good people of other faiths. The leader closed the Bible and moved to the next topic. Afterwards, three friends went for ice cream without him.
The following Sunday: Nobody sat next to him in the pew. Vikas felt so alone he drafted a message to the group saying he was done with all of them. He didn't send it. He went home and lay on the floor.
Two weeks later: Damini, a quiet girl from the choir, stopped him on the church steps. 'I heard your question. I've wondered the same.' She said old Father Pinto, who taught at the seminary, loved hard questions. That Wednesday they went to see him together. Father Pinto poured tea and said, 'Good. Let's read.' Vikas walked home feeling less alone. He still went to the youth group, sometimes. He went to Father Pinto's every Wednesday.

qa.q: What did the leader do when Vikas asked his question?
qa.a: The leader closed the Bible and moved to the next topic.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling the following Sunday?
qa.a: Vikas felt lonely and hurt, enough to draft a message quitting the group.

qa.q: What choice worked better than cutting all ties?
qa.a: Finding open-minded people, Damini and Father Pinto, and meeting them weekly while still going to the group sometimes.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt when she heard Vikas's question?
qa.a: Damini felt a quiet recognition, having wondered the same, and wanted him to know he wasn't alone.

grounding: Shows a church youth group turning cold after a question, the loneliness it brings, and finding an open peer and elder instead of breaking away in anger.

passage:
'So you're saying it officially now? Atheist?' Pooja asked, passing the chips.
'I think so,' Chinmay said. 'Agnostic, maybe. I just don't believe any of it the way I used to.'
'How does it feel?'
'Lighter. Honestly. Like I stopped pretending in my own head.' He paused. 'And a bit lonely. Everyone at home is doing Ganpati this week.'
'Are you going?'
'Yes. Aai would be so hurt if I didn't. And I like the modaks and the drumming. It's family.'
'Didn't you say rituals are just superstition last month?'
Chinmay winced. 'I did. I was being a smart-aleck. I felt clever for about a day.' He picked at the chips. 'I don't want to be that person. I want to be someone who's honest, keeps promises, is kind to Aai. Those I can name.'
'That's a better list than a lot of people have,' Pooja said.
'Don't say that at my house,' he laughed.

qa.q: What festival is everyone at home celebrating this week?
qa.a: Everyone at home is celebrating Ganpati.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel about calling himself an atheist?
qa.a: Chinmay feels lighter and relieved, but also a bit lonely with family celebrating.

qa.q: What values does Chinmay choose to live by?
qa.a: Being honest, keeping promises and being kind to Aai, while still joining the family's festival.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay's Aai be hurt if he skipped Ganpati?
qa.a: For her it is family and faith together, so his absence might feel like rejection.

grounding: Shows settling into non-belief with relief and some loneliness, choosing named values, and respecting the family's rituals instead of mocking them.

passage: I'm Dolma, and in my second year I decided I didn't believe in rebirth or anything else my grandmother taught me. It felt like taking off a heavy coat. I was relieved. I was also, if I'm honest, a little proud of myself, as if I had seen through something nobody else could. One evening in the hostel, Charu was keeping a fast for her fiancé, and I laughed and said, 'You know the moon doesn't care, right?' She didn't answer. Later I heard her on the phone, voice small, telling her mother she felt stupid. That stopped me. I had called myself rational and then been cruel. I knocked on her door and apologised. Now I try to live by things I can name: be truthful, don't harm, help when I can. I still light a butter lamp with my grandmother when I'm home, for her. I'm lonelier than I was. But I'm less proud, and kinder.

qa.q: What did Dolma say to Charu about the fast?
qa.a: Dolma said, 'You know the moon doesn't care, right?'

qa.q: How did Dolma feel after deciding not to believe?
qa.a: Dolma felt relieved, like taking off a heavy coat, and a little proud.

qa.q: What did Dolma learn to do instead of mocking?
qa.a: To apologise, respect Charu's practice, and live by named values like truthfulness and not harming.

qa.q: How did Charu feel after Dolma's remark?
qa.a: Charu felt small and stupid, telling her mother so on the phone.

grounding: A first-person account of settling into non-belief with relief and loneliness, catching the pride of being 'rational', and choosing respect and named values.

passage: Javier hadn't been sure about God since his father's long illness, but every Sunday evening in his tiny Madrid flat he still lit the candle his grandmother had given him and sat in silence for ten minutes. His flatmate Tariq noticed one night. 'I thought you said you don't believe anymore.' Javier shrugged. 'I don't know what I believe. But when I light it, my hands stop shaking. It's like a door into a quiet room.' Tariq sat down on the floor beside him. 'I still pray fajr most mornings, even on days I'm not sure anyone's listening. My uncle says showing up is what matters.' They sat together while the candle burned. After a while Javier added, 'I don't want to use it to hide, though. Last week I lit it just so I wouldn't have to think about Papá.' Tariq nodded. 'Then maybe next Sunday, light it and think about him.'

qa.q: Who gave Javier the candle?
qa.a: His grandmother gave Javier the candle.

qa.q: How does lighting the candle make Javier feel?
qa.a: It steadies him; his hands stop shaking and he feels calm, even without certainty.

qa.q: What balance does Tariq suggest?
qa.a: Keeping the practice but using it to face his feelings about his father, not to hide from them.

qa.q: How does Tariq relate to Javier's practice?
qa.a: Tariq understands it, since he still prays fajr on days he isn't sure anyone is listening.

grounding: Shows a young man who still lights a candle despite doubts because it steadies him, while not letting the ritual stand in for facing real questions.

passage: The staff prayer room at the district hospital in Thrissur was barely bigger than a cupboard, with a small brass lamp, a cross on one wall and a framed verse from the Quran on another. Seema, a second-year nursing student, stopped there before every night shift to light the lamp. She wasn't sure anymore what she believed; the ward had shown her too many things she couldn't explain. Joseph, from her batch, found her there at 9:55 one night. 'I didn't know you were religious.' 'I'm not sure I am,' she said. 'But lighting it steadies my hands before the ward. It's the one quiet minute I get.' Joseph nodded. 'I used to say the rosary without believing any of it. Now I just say it.' Seema laughed softly. Then she said, 'But I don't want this to replace asking questions. On my off day I'm going to talk to the chaplain and the old imam who visits. Both.' She went to the ward.

qa.q: At what time did Joseph find Seema in the prayer room?
qa.a: Joseph found her there at 9:55 one night.

qa.q: How does lighting the lamp make Seema feel?
qa.a: It steadies Seema's hands and gives her one calm, quiet minute before the ward.

qa.q: How does Seema keep the ritual from becoming a way to avoid questions?
qa.a: She plans to talk to the chaplain and the visiting imam on her off day.

qa.q: How does Joseph relate to Seema's practice?
qa.a: Joseph understands it, having said the rosary without believing, and now simply saying it.

grounding: Shows a nursing student who keeps lighting a lamp despite doubts because it steadies her, while still making room for real questions.

passage: It was the night before his thermodynamics exam, and Baljeet should have been asleep. Instead he was staring at Binita's latest post: a cartoon of people praying to a phone charger, captioned 'Same energy.' Forty people had laughed at it, including two from his class. He felt it like a slap. He did his ardaas every morning; it was part of who he was. His thumbs flew: a reply calling atheists 'arrogant, empty people'. He stopped before sending. Below her post, one comment stood out, from Binita herself: 'Serious question though, why do people pray if outcomes don't change?' That was a real question, buried under a joke. Baljeet deleted his draft. He wrote to her privately instead: 'The cartoon hurt, honestly. But your question is fair. I pray because it steadies me and reminds me whom I owe. Happy to talk after the exam.' Then he put the phone face down and slept. At lunch the next day, she came to find him.

qa.q: What did Binita's cartoon show?
qa.a: Binita's cartoon showed people praying to a phone charger.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel on seeing the post?
qa.a: Baljeet felt attacked, as if slapped, because prayer is part of who he is.

qa.q: How did Baljeet separate the mockery from the honest question?
qa.a: He dropped the angry reply, told Binita privately that the cartoon hurt, and answered her real question about why people pray.

qa.q: What does Binita coming to find Baljeet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was open to his answer and wanted to talk, perhaps sorry the cartoon hurt.

grounding: Shows a believer stung by a friend's online mockery, choosing to engage her honest question and leave the ridicule instead of answering contempt with contempt.

passage: At the canteen of their Delhi college, Raghav held his phone up to the table: a video of a man 'proving' prayer was useless by praying for a pizza. Everyone laughed. Hemant, who kept a Tuesday fast for Hanuman-ji, felt his stomach twist. Raghav turned to him. 'Come on, Hemant, you don't actually think the fast does anything?' The table went quiet, waiting. Hemant felt the old urge to fire back, to call Raghav's atheism just a fashion. Instead he said evenly, 'If you're asking seriously, I'll answer seriously. If it's for laughs, I'll pass.' Raghav blinked. 'Okay. Seriously. What does it do?' 'It's one day a week I practise saying no to myself. And it connects me to my grandfather, who kept the same fast.' Raghav was quiet, then said, 'That's fair, actually.' The others went back to their food. Later, walking to class, Raghav said, 'Sorry about the pizza video.'

qa.q: What did the video on Raghav's phone show?
qa.a: It showed a man praying for a pizza to 'prove' prayer was useless.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel when the table laughed?
qa.a: Hemant felt his stomach twist, hurt and defensive about his faith.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering a serious answer only to a serious question, which separated mockery from honest curiosity and kept things calm.

qa.q: How does Raghav's view change during the scene?
qa.a: Raghav moves from mocking to finding Hemant's answer fair, and later apologises.

grounding: Shows a believer mocked in front of friends, who refuses to answer contempt with contempt and engages only the honest question.

passage: My name is Vaibhav, and for months the words 'just have faith' made my jaw clench. My best friend Nitin said them every time I talked about my mother's surgery or my failed semester. I'd go quiet and think, That's not an answer, that's a slogan. Once I nearly told him his belief was a crutch for people who couldn't think. I'm glad I didn't. One night on the hostel terrace, instead of arguing, I asked him, 'What does faith actually give you, when you say that?' He took a long time to answer. He said it gave him a feeling that he wasn't carrying everything alone, and that when his father lost his job, it was the only thing that let him sleep. I didn't feel that. But I understood him better. Then I told him what I needed from him: not advice, just, 'That sounds hard, I'm here.' He said he'd try. He does, mostly.

qa.q: What words made Vaibhav's jaw clench?
qa.a: The words 'just have faith' made Vaibhav's jaw clench.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav feel when Nitin said 'just have faith'?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt irritated and unheard, as if Nitin were offering a slogan instead of an answer.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do instead of calling Nitin's belief a crutch?
qa.a: Vaibhav asked what faith gave Nitin, listened, and then said plainly what support Vaibhav needed.

qa.q: What does faith give Nitin, according to Nitin?
qa.a: A feeling that he isn't carrying everything alone, which helped him sleep when his father lost his job.

grounding: A first-person account of irritation at a devout friend's 'just have faith', and choosing to ask what faith gives him and to share one's own needs.

passage: Note from Rehana, NSS programme coordinator, after Saturday's village camp. Something small but worth recording. During the evening discussion, Sumit, a second-year volunteer, was talking about his grandfather's long illness. Faizan, his closest friend in the unit and a very devout young man, said, 'Just have faith, it'll be okay.' I saw Sumit's face tighten; he muttered, 'That's what people say when they've got nothing,' loud enough for a few to hear. Faizan went quiet. After the session I found Sumit by the water tank. I didn't scold him. I asked what he had needed in that moment. He said, 'Someone to just listen.' I suggested he tell Faizan that, and ask what faith means to Faizan, rather than judging it. Later, by the fire, I saw them sitting together. Sumit was doing most of the listening. Faizan's hand was on his shoulder. I'll check in with both at the next camp.

qa.q: What did Sumit mutter after Faizan spoke?
qa.a: Sumit muttered, 'That's what people say when they've got nothing.'

qa.q: What did Sumit's tight face suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggested Sumit felt irritated and hurt, wanting to be listened to rather than told to have faith.

qa.q: What did Rehana suggest Sumit do?
qa.a: Tell Faizan what he needed, someone to listen, and ask what faith means to Faizan instead of judging it.

qa.q: How might Faizan have felt when Sumit muttered the remark?
qa.a: Faizan likely felt hurt and embarrassed, since he meant his words as comfort.

grounding: A coordinator's note shows irritation at a devout friend's 'just have faith', and a nudge to ask what faith means to him and say what one needs.

passage:
Dear Akash,
You asked how the weekend at the ashram near Rishikesh was. Mixed, honestly.
The talks were beautiful. Swami-ji speaks about kindness in a way that made me cry once. But something bothered me. When a woman asked a simple question about where the donations go, three devotees told her to 'surrender her doubts'. Swami-ji just smiled and changed the topic. Everyone kept saying he was beyond mistakes. People touched the chair he had sat on.
I thought about our old music teacher, who used to say, 'If a student can't question me, I'm not teaching, I'm performing.' A real teacher, I think, welcomes questions, answers to someone, and doesn't need your wallet or your obedience.
I'm not saying Swami-ji is a fraud. I'm saying I'll go back only if questions are welcome.
Come with me next time and tell me what you see?
Rafiq

qa.q: What question did the woman ask?
qa.a: The woman asked where the donations go.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel during the weekend?
qa.a: Rafiq felt moved by the talks but uneasy about how questions were silenced.

qa.q: What test does Rafiq decide to use before going back?
qa.a: Whether questions are welcome, the teacher answers to someone, and no money or blind obedience is demanded.

qa.q: How do the devotees seem to see Swami-ji?
qa.a: They see him as beyond mistakes, even touching the chair he sat on.

grounding: A letter describes a teacher treated as beyond question by devotees, and Rafiq's test that a genuine teacher welcomes questions and asks no money or blind obedience.

passage: I'll tell you how I left, since everyone asks. I'm Hrithik, and at nineteen I'd have done almost anything our teacher asked. He ran meditation camps for college students in Bengaluru, and his senior disciple, Chaitanya, called him 'the living answer'. We gave up weekends, then small donations, then bigger ones. Nobody asked why. Then, at one camp, I asked in a question session why his trust's accounts weren't shared like other trusts' are. The room froze. Chaitanya took me aside and said questions like that came from 'a closed heart'. That night I lay awake, feeling guilty and also, underneath, clear. A good teacher would have answered. I called my cousin, who works at a charity, and she said genuine trusts publish their accounts. I stopped going. I still meditate. I just don't need anyone to be beyond question anymore.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya call the teacher?
qa.a: Chaitanya called him 'the living answer'.

qa.q: What did Hrithik feel lying awake that night?
qa.a: Hrithik felt guilty but also, underneath, clear that something was wrong.

qa.q: What sign told Hrithik the teacher might not be genuine?
qa.a: A fair question about the accounts was met with silence and blame instead of an answer.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Hrithik's question?
qa.a: Chaitanya treats it as coming from 'a closed heart', a fault in Hrithik rather than a fair question.

grounding: A spoken account of a teacher treated as beyond question, and Hrithik recognising that a genuine teacher would welcome questions and be accountable for money.

passage: In the dining hall of a spiritual centre outside Pune, Kalyani sat with her untouched rice. That morning she had told the group leader she wanted to go home for her sister's exams. 'That is your ego speaking,' the leader said gently. 'People who leave before the course ends invite misfortune on their families.' The words followed her all day. She felt guilty for doubting and frightened for her sister. In the evening free hour, the one time phones were allowed, she called her college friend Sabina. Her voice shook as she repeated the leader's words. Sabina was quiet, then said, 'Kalyani, a real teacher doesn't scare you into staying. That's fear and guilt being used on you.' She asked if Kalyani could talk to her parents before deciding anything. Kalyani called her mother that same evening. Her mother said, 'Come home. We'll talk here.' The next morning Kalyani packed her bag.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani want to go home?
qa.a: Kalyani wanted to go home for her sister's exams.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling after the leader's words?
qa.a: Kalyani felt guilty for doubting and frightened for her sister.

qa.q: What steps helped Kalyani decide?

passage:
Dear Pooja-di,
I need your honest view before I decide something, and I can't talk about it with anyone in the group.
For eight months I've been part of an online meditation circle. It helped at first; I slept better after Papa's surgery. But lately our teacher says that any doubt is 'the ego fighting the light'. Last week I said I wanted a break for my final exams. The senior member messaged me privately: 'People who step away often find accidents coming to their families. Think carefully.' I read it at 2 a.m. and couldn't sleep.
Part of me feels guilty for questioning. Part of me feels scared. And a small part is angry, because that's not how love sounds.
You've always been the calm one. Could we talk this weekend before I reply to them? I'd also like to tell Mummy, but I want to say it clearly first.
With love,
Vandana

qa.q: What is the senior member's message trying to do?
qa.a: It uses fear about accidents to make Vandana feel guilty and stay in the group.

grounding: A letter shows a circle calling doubt ego and hinting at misfortune for leaving, and Vandana turning to family outside the group before deciding.
